headline: A Goodfire researcher argues in a new essay that the inner workings of AI models are far easier to read than the field believed, and other experts are split on whether he is right.
score_reason: Notable dispute in a core AI safety research field; claims are preliminary and not yet confirmed by others.
importance_line: If the claim holds it would make it easier to check whether an AI model is deceptive or behaving dangerously, which matters to safety researchers and anyone relying on these systems, but the results are preliminary, come from a company with a stake in the idea and are already doubted by Google DeepMind's Neel Nanda.
summary: The Decoder reports that Nick Cammarata, a researcher at the interpretability lab Goodfire, argues in an essay that single neurons in AI models mostly have one clear job, rejecting the widely held idea of superposition, in which a network packs unrelated concepts into the same neurons, and gives early figures for the Qwen3-32B model in which about 90 percent of the neuron poles he counted have one main job. OpenAI's Roon, an employee who posts under that pseudonym on X, calls it a possible major moment in scientific history, while Neel Nanda, who leads the interpretability team at Google DeepMind, says it does not really change the big picture, and the companion technical paper has not yet been released.
notes: Read in full from The Decoder. Interpretability means tracing how a model reaches its answers; this is explained in the Why it matters line only by implication.
